Chela James.

Senior Bioinformatician/Data Scientist at Human Technopole

ORCID in LinkedIn

01 / Work

Career development

  • From molecular biology to bioinformatics

    Around 2011 I switched from molecular biology to bioinformatics, since completing my PhD for many years I had been a molecular biologist, up until that point all the computing I did was limited to microsoft windows. While working on a postdoc on the genetic basis of hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia my PI handed me an external hard disk drive with some patient whole-exome sequence data. I took on the challenge, converted my desktop PC to Linux and learned the command line and the myriad tools required to align sequence data, call variants and annotate them. This led to the identification of some candidate genes, and I was hooked.

    The next role I took on was as bioinformatician for GOSgene, a team which processed genome sequences from clinical samples with the aim of identifying rare inherited disorders. My knowledge of bioinformatics expanded to the use of high performance computing clusters, cloud computing and the use of workflow management systems.

02 / Milestones

Selected projects

  • 2026

    Italian genomics

    I currently work for The Human Technopole National Facility for Data Handling and Analysis (NF-DHA) which is a new facility that provides the Italian scientific community with access to high-performance computing resources and expertise in data analysis. I currently develop the bioinformatics pipelines and data analysis workflows for the facility, which supports a wide range of research projects in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and other omics fields. What is exciting about this role is the diversity of the projects that I get to work on: Topics range from single-cell transcriptomics to population genomics, from the survival of baboon species to cancer genomics.

    AI, Machine learning and agentic programming

    Artificial intelligence has offered a myriad of new methods of working and I am very curious about exploiting it to improve our analyses. One example of what I am pursuing is in quality control. I routinely process thousands of samples and on the whole they pass QC. Having seqera or openai ai tools examine them all would be costly. I have created a script that surveys a MultiQC output and picks out the outliers, only the selected outliers are then submitted to the seqera or openai agents to speculate about the reasons why they stand out. Another project that interests me is using machine learning to rescue variant calls that have been rejected on the basis of quality by leveraging the hundreds of other samples that have been processed the same way.

  • 2019

    Lots of data

    During my time in the Sottoriva lab, in order to standardise and make their processing more efficient, I introduced the Nextflow pipeline system to their data processing and analysis. As well as all the analyses, data needs organising, so one of my tasks was to ensure that the pipelines output the files in a logical structure and a database is used to track the samples, their metadata and the processing status. It occurred to me that a simple json schema which is easy to access and update would be a suitable solution for this scale of data handling.

  • 2016

    What happens when blood starts to flow?

    As a bioinformatician my guiding principle is understanding the science and having the flexibility to attempt new methods and present data in clear and interesting ways. One example of this is my collaboration with Emanuele Azzoni and Marella de Bruijn in this paper: onset of circulation triggers a metabolic switch required for endothelial to hematopoietic transition. My goal was to process the single-cell transcriptomic data and present it in, for example, a useable notebook format

  • 2002

    First PostDoc

    I published Tooth development is independent of a Hox patterning programme This work was very interesting on the level of developmental biology and the role of the Hox genes and also technically challenging.

  • 1999

    My PhD Project

    This was a speculative project searching for a novel neurotransmitter protein. Diverse methodologies were employed including molecular biology techniques including southern blotting and microinjection of constructs into the model organism C.elegans.

03 / hobbies

Outside work

  • Languages

    I have a passion for languages and have studied several over the years. Learning Italian gives me a window into the culture, at lunchtime at work my colleagues can relax and chat in Italian and I can join in. It also gives me an opportunity to read books in their original language letting me appreciate some of the nuances that may be lost in translation.
